title: News Classification Pipeline
role: Pipeline design, data-quality controls and evaluation workflow
summary: A leakage-aware multiclass news classifier built around schema validation, duplicate analysis, drift checks, sparse text features and stratified cross-validation.
proof_detail: Evaluation discipline and data-quality controls are first-class stages of the pipeline.
visual_alt: News classification pipeline showing schema and leakage checks, sparse text and metadata features, cross-validation, model selection and reporting.
problem: Text classification can look strong for the wrong reasons when duplicates, source effects or train/evaluation overlap leak label information. The project is structured around making the reported validation defensible before choosing a classifier.
built: The workflow validates schemas, audits duplicates and overlap, checks development/evaluation drift, removes cross-label duplicate problems, combines word and character TF-IDF with source, ranking, timestamp and missingness features, then compares linear models under stratified cross-validation.

decisions.title: Audit before modeling.
decisions.text: Duplicate, overlap, missingness and drift checks happen before model selection so suspicious signal is visible instead of buried inside a score.

decisions.title: Use sparse models that fit the data.
decisions.text: Word and character TF-IDF plus metadata form one sparse design matrix, making Linear SVM a deliberate baseline rather than reaching for a larger neural model by default.

decisions.title: Record fold-level evidence.
decisions.text: Cross-validation outputs include per-class metrics, confusion matrices, out-of-fold counts and fold diagnostics rather than one train/test number.

results.label: evaluation
results.detail: stratified CV with per-class and fold-level diagnostics

results.label: unified entry point
results.detail: the complete path includes leakage cleaning before training

constraints: The repository does not present a single headline test score as the project's main claim.
Model choice is intentionally conservative: linear sparse models are a strong fit for the feature space.
The value of the project is the defensible workflow around messy text inputs, not architectural novelty.
